title: Elastic micro-window preemption and soft-commit experiments
content:
Purpose / quick summary:

This note captures the design, runs, and early analysis for a set of experiments exploring an "elastic micro-window" approach to continuous request coalescing plus a lightweight preemption/soft-commit mechanism. Goal: reduce 99/99.9 p99 tail latency for mixed short+long sequence workloads while preserving aggregate throughput and fairness across tenants.

Context / motivation:
- Continuous coalescers (our default path) do well on throughput but show long tails when a small fraction of requests have long token counts or when arrival patterns form microbursts.
- Existing timeout-based flushes can either be too aggressive (wasteful small batches -> cost) or too late (tail latency spikes).
- Prior experiments looked at adaptive timeouts and urgency-weighted heuristics; this run focuses on hybrid sizing (micro-windows) + preemption where a long-running batch can be soft-committed and split when high-priority short requests appear.

Key terms used here (informal):
- micro-window: a short, sliding window (e.g. 1-4ms) used to decide whether to accept new requests into an active batch before kernel enqueue. Elastic means the window increases if arrivals are sparse and shrinks when busy.
- soft-commit: marking an in-flight batch as "commit soon" such that we stop accepting new low-priority requests but allow the current token generation to finish for already queued requests; the batch can be split on next safe boundary to pull out high-priority arrivals.
- preemption-slab: the mechanism that allows a small subset of requests to be promoted to the next batch by pausing/duplicating some internal bookkeeping, not cancelling GPU work.

Experiment hypotheses:
1) An elastic micro-window that shrinks in high-arrival regimes will significantly reduce p99 for short requests in mixed workloads without increasing cost more than 3–5%.
2) Soft-commit + preemption slab will reduce spike P99 from long requests interrupting short ones, provided we limit promotions to <= 5% of tokens per second per instance to avoid kernel thrash.
3) Combining both yields better fairness (per-tenant p95/p99 delta reduced) than either alone.

Bench setup:
- Cluster: 6x A100s on test fleet (dedicated test pool); same kernel build as prod (rev: gc7d12b).
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production replay traces:
  * Mix A (front-door): 85% short (<=16 tokens), 10% medium (50–150), 5% long (500–1500)
  * Mix B (search-like): 60% short, 25% medium, 15% long
  * Mix C (burst-mix): sustained 1k rps with 10% microbursts at 4-8k rps for 15s every 2 min
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (enqueue->first-byte, and enqueue->complete), per-tenant p50/p95/p99/p99.9, batch size distribution, kernel occupancy, token-cost per request, and interrupts/splits count.
- Instrumentation hooks: trace ids propagated to microtrace collector, event markers for window open/close, soft-commit toggle, preemption events.

Variants tested:
- V0 (baseline): current continuous coalescer (timeout=8ms, no preemption).
- V1: fixed micro-window 2ms, no elasticity, no preemption.
- V2: elastic micro-window (min=1ms, max=6ms) size adapts to arrival rate using exponential moving average of inter-arrival time.
- V3: V2 + soft-commit enabled (max promotions per second capped), split-on-safe-boundary set to token boundary.
- V4: V3 + fairness steering: clients with >2x observed p99 get preferential promotion budget.

Preliminary results (summary of runs on Mix A/B):
- V1 vs V0: p99 for short requests improved ~12–15% but average batch size shrank 8% -> token cost up 2.1%.
- V2 vs V1: elastic sizing recovered some batch size (batch size only -3% vs baseline) while keeping p99 improvement ~13%. Cost delta ~+0.7%.
- V3 vs V2: short-request p99 improved further (~25% vs baseline); long-request completion tail slightly increased for the promoted medium requests but overall throughput stable. Preemption events averaged 3.7% of requests and promotions limited to 4% of tokens/sec.
- V4: fairness steering reduced inter-tenant p99 skew; tenants previously penalized by background long tails saw ~30% reduction in their p99, while global p99 same as V3.

Observations and interesting traces:
- Trace 1423 (Mix A, V3) shows a 3-way split where a long 1200-token request kept the batch open; three short incoming requests at t+3.8ms triggered soft-commit and promotions. The kernel recorded a slight increase in dispatch overhead (8–12us) but client-observed first-byte latency for short requests dropped from 210ms to 42ms.
- We saw occasional kernel-level jitter when promotions coincide with large KV-cache writes; these correlate with high memory churn and can be mitigated by delaying cache writes to post-token-commit in the caller thread.
- Promotion budget policy matters: greedy promotion yields fairness but increases kernel CPU jitter; conservative caps keep kernel stable but some tenants still see tail spikes.

Open questions / risks:
- Safety of splitting on arbitrary token boundaries for some model families (autoregressive hazards). Need model-aware splitting (e.g., only split between sentences for longer context models).
- Impact on decoder caching—preemption may increase KV cache churn if we duplicate contexts across batches. Quantify cache miss delta.
- Billing implications: promotions might increase token accounting complexity (partial tokens?). Need accounting policy decisions with finance.

Action items (next steps):
- Short term (this sprint):
  1) Run longer-duration Mix C replay for V3/V4 to validate stability under microbursts (Marco). Target: 48h continuous run.
  2) Add lightweight model-aware split guard: consult tokenizer boundaries before splitting (Priya).
  3) Add a metric for KV-cache duplicate entries and correlate with promotion events (Evan).
- Medium term:
  1) Integrate promotion budget into quota system so we can A/B customer-visible fairness (product).
  2) Prototype accounting rule for partial promotions and cost attribution; sync with finance.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could combine preemption with a tiny speculative model runner for super-short completions (<8 tokens): dispatch speculative short-run to a low-latency path and then cancel if long path yields output first. Dangerous but interesting for front-door UX.
- Consider telemetry flag to mark model families where splitting is prohibited (e.g., models with complex stateful decoding).

References / links inside cluster:
- replay traces: s3://replay/mixA/2024-09-replay.tar.gz
- microtrace dashboard: /dash/serving/microwindow-preempt/v3
- related tickets: RINF-3241 (scheduler work), RINF-3308 (billing accounting)

Draft conclusions (tentative):
- Elastic micro-windows plus a carefully-capped soft-commit/preemption slab materially reduce short-request tails in mixed workloads with modest cost increase when tuned properly.
- Operational stability hinges on promotion budgeting and KV-cache duplication control.
- Next milestone: 48h Mix C stability run + tokenizer-aware split validator.
